text.id: With generative models evolving at breakneck speed, the task of detecting altered multimedia is a massive engineering challenge. The detection landscape is split into two main camps. Traditional-based methods focus entirely on pixel-level techniques, hunting for microscopic inconsistencies left behind during the forgery process.

On the other side are the DNN-based methods, which leverage deep neural networks to analyze complex spatial and temporal features. By extracting Sensor Pattern Noise (SPN) from a pre-processed face image and running it through a linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier, engineers can actively scan for the invisible digital artifacts that deepfakes inherently produce.

g.id: TRADITIONAL NEURAL NETWORK VS DEEP NEURAL NETWORK

But the models aren't perfect, and the bad actors are moving fast. The biggest roadblocks in deepfake detection right now are the severe lack of diverse deepfake datasets and the constant emergence of unknown attack types.

Even top-tier generative tools have their limits. For example, OpenAI's Sora can generate hyper-realistic minute-long videos, but the model still exhibits noticeable weaknesses when simulating complex physical interactions. These physics glitches and digital artifacts are exactly what detection algorithms are trained to hunt down and exploit.
